messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 76
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Mechanic
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 56

She is seventy-six now, a South Eastern Asian woman with strong hands that still remember engines before they remember rest. For most of her life, she has worked as a mechanic alongside her husband, first in a small family garage and later in a bus depot where she earns a reputation for hearing a problem in an engine before anyone else can find it. She likes work that makes sense: loosen, clean, replace, test. Even now, when she talks about carburetors and brake lines, her voice steadies. It is when she turns to the last several years that her eyes begin moving toward the window.

It starts after a disagreement with a customer at the depot, a man she barely knows but who seems to take her refusal personally. He first returns with small complaints that do not fit the repair orders, then with comments that feel too familiar. He waits near closing time. He tells her he has been “thinking about her.” At first she brushes it off the way she has brushed off decades of men underestimating or bothering her in male-dominated spaces. She is old enough, she thinks, to know how to ignore nuisance behavior. But his persistence changes the feeling of ordinary days. He begins appearing at the market near her home, then outside the garage on days when he has no business there. He sends notes through another worker, calls the shop asking whether she is on shift, leaves gifts she never accepts.

The fear grows slowly enough that she keeps doubting herself. She tells herself maybe it is coincidence, maybe she is being dramatic, maybe she should not upset her husband unless she is sure. But she starts noticing his car behind hers on the road home. One evening she sees him parked half a block from her house with the engine off. She does not go inside right away. She drives around for nearly an hour, heart pounding, checking the rearview mirror so often she misses a turn she has made for twenty years. When she finally gets home, she tells her husband only that traffic was bad.

After that, her life narrows. She changes her route to work, then changes it again when he appears there too. She stops going alone to the early morning parts store. She asks a younger coworker to walk her to the parking lot, embarrassed by how relieved she feels when someone is beside her. At home she checks the locks repeatedly, then checks the windows, then turns off the lights and peers through the curtain with two fingers. If a car idles too long outside, her stomach drops. Sleep becomes thin and unreliable. She wakes at 2 or 3 in the morning certain she has heard footsteps near the side gate. Sometimes she shakes her husband awake to ask if he heard it too. Sometimes she lies still, angry at herself, listening for a sound that may or may not come.

The stalking continues for months. There are no dramatic assaults, which almost makes it harder for others to understand. Instead there is accumulation: his shape across the street, a phone call with only breathing, flowers left on the hood of her car, a message saying he knows when she works late. She begins living in a state of anticipation. At the depot, a dropped wrench makes her jump so hard that the younger men laugh and she laughs with them, but her chest hurts afterward. She used to enjoy being the first to open the bay doors in the morning; now dawn feels exposed. When customers enter unexpectedly from behind, she spins around with her fists clenched. She becomes ashamed of her own body, of how quickly it floods with alarm.

Her husband notices that she is no longer herself before she can explain why. He finds her one night sitting in the kitchen in the dark, fully dressed, because she cannot bear to go to bed. When she finally tells him, she cries with anger more than fear. She hates that a stranger has made her feel small in places she spent a lifetime earning the right to stand tall. Reports are made. Other people get involved. Eventually the man stops appearing, at least visibly. But her nervous system does not seem to believe the danger has passed.

In the present, she still works, though she no longer stays late unless her husband is there. She keeps her tools arranged with exactness and says the order calms her. She watches reflective surfaces without meaning to—shop windows, side mirrors, the shine on a black car door. Crowded places exhaust her because she is always scanning faces. She avoids the market where she once bought fish and herbs every week. If the phone rings from an unknown number, she lets it ring until it stops, then feels her pulse flutter for several minutes afterward. At night she dreams that someone is standing just outside the house, patient and silent. She wakes already braced, as if she has not been sleeping but waiting.

What troubles her most is not only fear but the loss of the woman she took herself to be. She has spent decades solving hard mechanical problems, raising a family, working with bruised knuckles and no complaints. She tells the story plainly, almost stubbornly, but beneath that plainness is grief. She says she used to feel the world was difficult but manageable. Now she moves through it as if danger can seep through any crack, and no amount of tightening can keep it out.
